sections.h2: What should a seller know about North Carolina before opening a local guide?
sections.html:
Selling here means working with several county desks in turn. One office values the parcel, another bills the tax, the register of deeds files the sale, and the clerk of superior court oversees foreclosures and estates. This overview maps those desks so you know whom to call first.

Statewide law fixes some things, such as the recording fee schedule and the excise rate on deeds. Counties control the rest, including tax rates, hearing calendars and office procedures, so the city and county guides on this site carry the local detail.

sections.h2: How large is the North Carolina housing market?
sections.html:
Census estimates put the state at 11,197,968 people in mid-2025, about 7.2% more than the 2020 base. Owners hold 66.6% of housing units, and the middle owner-occupied home was worth $288,900 in the 2020 to 2024 survey period.

Renters and owners face different price levels: median gross rent is $1,228 a month, while median owner costs run $1,631 with a mortgage and $490 without one. North Carolina issued 86,167 building permits in 2025 and counted 5,168,052 housing units at mid-year. A mountain county, a coastal county and a Triangle suburb will each sit far from these medians, so ask the county tax office for the appraised value and tax history of the exact parcel you plan to sell.

sections.h2: How different are North Carolina counties from each other?
sections.html:
The state's county directory lists land areas from 221 square miles in Clay County to 1,562 square miles in Dare County, with county seats and founding years beside each entry.

The earliest counties on the list date from 1668: Chowan, Currituck, Pasquotank and Perquimans. The youngest are Avery and Hoke, both created in 1911. Later additions came in clusters: Swain in 1871, Graham and Pamlico in 1872, Scotland in 1899, Lee in 1907, and Durham and Vance, both in 1881. Duplin County (seat Kenansville, 819 square miles, formed 1750) and Durham County (298 square miles, formed 1881) differ in size and age, so expect office hours, forms and online search tools to vary from one county to the next. Call the register of deeds in your own county before you plan a recording, and ask whether it takes appointments or walk-ins for closings. A parcel in an older county can have a longer paper trail at the register of deeds, which is worth knowing before a title search begins.

sections.h2: Which North Carolina county seats are easy to miss?
sections.html:
In many counties the courthouse sits in a small town with a different name from the county, so check the seat before you plan a deed signing or an estate filing. The nc.gov directory shows several of these.

  • Brunswick County is served from Bolivia.
  • Rockingham County is served from Wentworth.
  • Polk County is served from Columbus, and Tyrrell County from Columbia.
  • Pender County is served from Burgaw, Pamlico County from Bayboro and Hyde County from Swan Quarter.
  • Hertford County is served from Winton, while Perquimans County is served from the town named Hertford.

Among larger metros, Wake County spans 857 square miles around Raleigh, Guilford 658 around Greensboro and Buncombe 660 around Asheville, while Durham County covers just 298 and New Hanover 328. Forsyth County (Winston-Salem) covers 413 and Cumberland (Fayetteville) 658. Large rural counties can mean a long drive to the courthouse. Dare, Hyde and Carteret each exceed 1,300 square miles, and Beaufort County covers 959 square miles with its seat in Washington.

sections.h2: Where does a North Carolina deed get recorded, and at what cost?
sections.html:
Voters elect a register of deeds in every county every two years, and that office files the deed for land in its county. Whoever transfers the property pays the excise tax first, at one dollar for every five hundred of price or part thereof.

  • A typical instrument costs $26.00 for its first fifteen pages and $4.00 for each page after that.
  • A mortgage or deed of trust costs $64.00 for its first thirty-five pages, plus $4.00 per extra page.
  • Cancelling a deed of trust or mortgage carries no recording fee.

Registration also sets priority. An unrecorded deed, option or long lease gives no protection against lien creditors or buyers who paid value, and the earlier recording wins.

sections.h2: How does the North Carolina property tax year run?
sections.html:
Owners list property in January, and bills arrive for payment by the first day of September. Interest begins on January 6 at 2%, followed by three-fourths of one percent for each month starting in February.

Value disputes start with the commissioners sitting as a review board in spring. A taxpayer who loses there has a second stop, the state Property Tax Commission, and a written notice is due within a month of the county's mailed ruling. Every county must reappraise on an eight-year cycle at most. Ask your assessor which year your parcel was last revalued.

sections.h2: What do North Carolina household figures say about buyers and sellers?
sections.html:
QuickFacts counts 4,282,345 households for 2020 to 2024 at 2.44 people each, with 87.3% of residents in the same home as a year before. Median income per household is $72,388 in 2024 dollars, and a commute averages 25.1 minutes.

Residents aged 65 and older make up 18.9% of the population. Sellers of long-held homes can carry old repairs, unrecorded family transfers or estate paperwork, which is why the statewide probate and tax guides sit beside the county pages.

sections.h2: Which North Carolina office handles foreclosure, probate and eviction?
sections.html:
The courts handle all three, in different rooms. Foreclosure here is by power of sale, heard by the clerk of superior court after a notice period of at least ten days. A reported sale stays open to a higher bid for ten more days.

The same elected clerk acts as probate judge for estates. Evictions are filed in small claims before a magistrate, and the usual wait for a hearing is 10 to 15 days. Our statewide pages on probate, landlord and tenant law, and the homestead exclusion take each process in turn.

sections.h2: How do the guides for North Carolina fit together?
sections.html:
The statewide guides explain the law once: probate, foreclosure, eviction, tax sales, squatters and the elderly or disabled exclusion. County guides then cover the register of deeds in that county and its property tax process, and city guides describe selling a house in a particular town.

If the right page is unclear, start from the county where the property sits, since that county sets the bill, keeps the deed index and runs the clerk's office. Land that spans two counties is taxed at conveyance in the county holding the greater value, so confirm the filing office with the register of deeds before closing.

faqs.q: How many residents does North Carolina have?
faqs.a: About 11.2 million people, with the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate at 11,197,968, a gain of 7.2% since 2020.

faqs.q: Who files a deed for North Carolina land?
faqs.a: The register of deeds for the land's county. The seller settles the excise tax there first.

faqs.q: When does North Carolina property tax come due?
faqs.a: On September 1, with the penalty-free window closing January 5.

faqs.q: Where can an owner challenge a North Carolina valuation?
faqs.a: Request a hearing from the county board of equalization and review in spring. If you lose, the Property Tax Commission is the next step.

faqs.q: Where is a North Carolina foreclosure heard?
faqs.a: Before the clerk of superior court where the house stands, under the power-of-sale process.
